_comment: Short 6 in docs/CONTENT.md: billed, allowed, your share — three numbers, and only one is real. It explains the number behind the product's most common finding: 53 of 68 audits flagged billing above the EOB allowed amount.
_injury: A splinter, and a bandaid. The gap between the treatment and the number is the joke.
_numbers: $2,000 billed, $300 allowed, $60 your share. The 20% is named as the plan's coinsurance, not dropped in: an earlier cut said 'at twenty percent' with no source, which is the same mistake Short 2 v1 made with its split.
_analogy: The car sticker price, straight after the definition. 'Sticker price' is a car term to begin with, so the comparison is the word's own home: nobody pays the number on the window, someone always negotiates it down, and here the insurer did the negotiating years before you walked in. It replaced a hotel rack-rate analogy, which was true but further from the phrase.
_distinct: Short 1 is which paper is which; Short 5 is being billed for the discount. This one only sorts out which of the three numbers is real, and never mentions disputing anything.

variants.splinter: A splinter. One pair of tweezers, one bandaid. The bill says two thousand dollars.

body.text: Nobody pays that. Not you, and not your insurance.
If the clinic is in your network, your insurance already has its own price for that visit. Three hundred dollars.
That is the allowed amount, and it is the only number here that is real.
The two thousand is a sticker price. It exists so there is something to discount.
Like the sticker price on a car. Nobody pays it. Someone always negotiates it down.
Here, your insurance did the negotiating, years before you walked in.
Your share comes out of the three hundred, not the two thousand. Your plan says you pay twenty percent of it, so sixty dollars.
So when a bill looks enormous, read the letter before you panic. Out of network, the rules are different.
Check yours before you dispute. Or upload them free at UseClaimRight.com.

_network: The allowed amount is the insurer's negotiated price with a clinic IN its network, so the condition is stated with the number in m3 and written on the board beside the allowed bar. Out of network the provider is not bound by it and can bill the difference, which is Short 5's subject, so m9 says so rather than leaving the viewer to assume.
